name: Data Science and Analytics
guide:
Data Science and Analytics work centers on turning a company's existing data into decisions people can act on. A typical day might mean pulling data with SQL, building a model or a metric in Python, and then presenting what changed and why to a product or business team. This is different from Machine Learning Engineering, where the job is building and maintaining the systems that serve models in production at scale. It also differs from Data Engineering, which focuses on building the pipelines that move and clean data before a data scientist ever touches it. In our postings, roles titled simply Data Scientist are usually attached to a business function, like growth, pricing, trust and safety, or search quality, rather than to infrastructure.

Most postings in our data expect at least a bachelor's degree, and many prefer a master's in statistics, economics, applied math, or a related quantitative field. A handful of senior and staff titles at research-heavy companies favor a PhD, but this is the exception rather than the rule across our sample. We did not find named certifications, such as a specific cloud or analytics credential, listed as a requirement in the postings we reviewed. Employers in this data appear to weigh a strong academic record and demonstrated project work over any single certificate.

Junior data scientist openings are rare in our data, making up a small share of postings, and usually ask for one to two years of hands-on analysis experience or a strong internship background. The largest group of postings sits at the mid level, generally asking for roughly three to six years of experience building models, running experiments, and working directly with a business partner. Senior roles typically want five to eight years and the ability to own a metric or a product area with less oversight. Staff, principal, and director titles, which together make up a meaningful slice of our postings, expect eight or more years and a track record of setting technical direction across teams.

Python and SQL are by far the two most common named skills in our postings, each appearing far more often than any other tool. AWS shows up frequently too, alongside large language model experience, which is now a common addition to data science postings rather than a specialty on its own. Scala, Spark, and Databricks appear often as well, reflecting how much of this work runs against large scale data platforms. Azure, GCP, dbt, MLOps, and PyTorch round out the list of frequently named tools, though none of them approach the frequency of Python or SQL. Notably, R and traditional BI tools like Tableau or Power BI did not appear as named skills in the postings we tracked, even though many data scientists use them in day to day work.

We currently track approximately 106 open postings in Data Science and Analytics on theworldofai.org. Of the 352 postings we have analyzed in this category, 132 listed a specific annual salary range, and among those the figures ran from about 50,460 dollars to 373,680 dollars, with typical ranges clustering between roughly 130,000 and 179,000 dollars. OpenAI is the most frequent employer in our data with 18 postings, followed by McKinsey and Company with 16, Johnson and Johnson Innovative Medicine with 12, and Walmart and Waymo tied at 10 each. Lockheed Martin, Anthropic, and Databricks also post repeatedly for this discipline. Together this points to a market where established technology, consulting, and industrial firms and newer AI native companies are all actively hiring for this discipline.
